mappings.note: Plastic-handled screwdrivers and rubber gloves are the insulator idea worked into an electrician's daily practice. Not LO-34, because the materials are already named and the item asks why the practice exists.
Picks the statements that correctly characterise metals as a class, which is classification by properties. Not LO-33, because the item builds a general profile rather than identifying one material.
Names the brown deposit on iron as rust, identification of a material from its appearance. Not LO-37, because no cause is asked for.
Air and water together as the conditions for rusting is the phenomenon tied to its causes, which the three-bottle experiment established.
Silica gel is in bottle A to keep the air dry, so the item tests why the experiment is set up that way. Investigation design, not LO-37.
Boiled and cooled water under an oil layer excludes dissolved oxygen: again the logic of the control, which belongs to conducting the investigation.
Corrosion defined as metal decaying through reaction with air, water or the surroundings; the definition carries the cause, so it sits with the phenomenon-and-cause outcome rather than LO-33.
The green coating on corroded copper, recognised by its colour.
The black tarnish on silver, the companion colour-recognition item.
Painting, oiling, greasing and galvanising are listed as ways to stop iron rusting, which is the preventing-corrosion application named in LO-45.
Galvanisation as a zinc coat on iron: a named corrosion-prevention technique. Not LO-34, because zinc and iron are not being told apart.
The rust-free Iron Pillar as evidence of advanced ancient Indian metallurgy is a story of scientific achievement to be appreciated. Not LO-45, because no prevention method is asked for.
What is seen when magnesium ribbon burns, dazzling flame and white powder, is the recorded observation of the demonstration.
Naming magnesium oxide as the product of magnesium burning in air is the metal plus oxygen reaction that LO-39 covers. Not LO-36, because the item asks for the product rather than what was seen.
The litmus result for dissolved magnesium oxide is the evidence step of the demonstration. The generalisation it supports is tested separately.
Generalises from magnesium to all metal oxides being basic, which is placing a whole class of materials by a property. Not LO-36, because the evidence step is a different item.
Sodium is picked out of four metals by how violently it reacts and by needing kerosene storage: discrimination on a chemical property.
Sulfur dioxide as the product of burning sulfur, the non-metal plus oxygen reaction. Same outcome as the magnesium oxide item and for the same reason.
Dissolving the gas and reading the litmus gives the acidic verdict: the evidence step of the sulfur demonstration, matching the magnesium oxide item.
Generalises to non-metal oxides being acidic, the class-level counterpart of the metal oxide generalisation.
Phosphorus picked out from four non-metals by igniting in air and so being kept under water: property-based discrimination, like the sodium item.
Chooses the property set that characterises non-metals, a class profile rather than a single identification.
An element as a substance that cannot be broken down further is the category under which metals and non-metals both sit, so the classification outcome is the closest fit the frame offers.
Oxygen as the non-metal life depends on for respiration. First of a run of items in this batch on what particular non-metals are used for, all of which the frame houses in LO-45.
Carbon as the backbone of proteins, fats and carbohydrates: the same use-and-importance outcome.
Nitrogen as the fertiliser element for plant growth, again a use of a non-metal.
Chlorine for purifying water, a use in everyday life.
Iodine solution as an antiseptic on wounds, the last of the non-metal use items.
Alloys defined as mixtures of metals, or of a metal with a non-metal, which places a group of materials by composition. Not LO-45, because no use is asked for.
Aluminium for food packaging because it is malleable, cheap and easily shaped: property behind an everyday use.
Assertion and reason both concern metal oxides being basic and the litmus evidence for it; the knowledge tested is the class property, so LO-35.
Gold and silver for jewellery, justified by lustre, workability and resistance to corrosion. Property put to use, so LO-45.
Magnesium oxide basic against sulfur dioxide acidic is an explicit metal-versus-non-metal contrast, so LO-34 rather than the two class-generalisation items on LO-35.
Copper chosen for a pan because it conducts heat best of the listed materials: a property applied to a household object.
Oil keeps both air and water off the nail, so it does not rust: corrosion prevention, named in LO-45. Not LO-37, because the item asks why the treatment works rather than what rusting requires.
Why sulfur cannot replace zinc for galvanising: a judgement about a corrosion-prevention coating, so LO-45 rather than LO-34.
Names malleability, property vocabulary tied to what is observed when a material is hammered.
Gold and silver named as the most malleable metals: materials identified by degree of a property.
Brittle as the term for materials that shatter under a hammer.
Names ductility as the drawing-into-wire property.
Gold identified from the one-gram-to-two-kilometre ductility figure.
Names sonority as the ringing property of metals.
States that metals as a class conduct heat well. A class-level property, so LO-35; the spoon items that set metal against wood are on LO-34.
Non-metals as poor conductors of electricity, the class-level counterpart of the previous item.
Mercury named as the metal liquid at room temperature, identification by an observable state.
